Pat on the Bacchae for National Theatre’s new director with flamboyant debut … Indhu Rubasingham’s first staging is radical but has a saving streak of psychological insight … It’s a relief to report that Rubasingham – the first person of colour and the first woman to run the NT – passes her high-pressure test in surprisingly flamboyant style (aided by a shifting set of giant slabs by designer Robert Jones), and, though it takes time to emerge, with a saving dollop of substance. … Some people may develop an allergy to Taleghani’s loosely rhyming, militantly unstuffy way with words and fourth-wall breaking familiarity... This messy rap-infused riff on Euripides’s tragedy is a fun way to kick off Indhu Rubasingham’s National Theatre tenure … Arguably the entire point of the first play to be programmed at the National Theatre by its new boss Indhu Rubasingham comes around five minutes from the end... And if the hour and 40 minutes that precede this moment are messy, I’d say they are entertainingly messy. … ... colourful, irreverent and frequently goofy, its sillier moments reminded me of those hip hop Shakespeare plays that sometimes pop up at the Edinburgh Fringe … It’s fun to spend time with them, as they swear and argue and rage, but there’s the nagging sense that it’s not clear where their story is going. Half really cool, half really naff … The first play under new National Theatre Director Indhu Rubasingham is production of wild mood swings that ticks off issues but loses the plot … If it were a triumph, life would be easier; the National in safe hands, theatre saved. If it were a dud everyone could cluck and crow. Instead it’s both, and also everything in between. Refugees, feminism, gender, sexuality, dictators, set to rap and dance…this is a production of wild mood swings, mediated through a production whose beauty often outstrips its substance. … Clare Perkins is their brilliantly ferocious, no-fucks-given leader Vida … ... the political resonances have the subtlety of a fist to the face. Rocky start to Indhu Rubasingham’s National Theatre reign nonetheless proves she’s committed to bold programming … It proves a big ask of the debuting Taleghani to write a version of one of the great tragedies for the National’s vast Olivier Theatre. While there’s certainly lyricism and gumption to his adaptation, much of which is written in verse, it’s a disjointed offering with add-ins that distract from the story. More confusingly, until its final grisly throes, too much effort is spent on making it funny. … It opens promisingly with a striking image: designer Robert Jones sends the giant head of a white horse, streaked with blood, galloping towards the audience from above the stage... A tragedy of blunders as leaden update falls flat … The actor Nima Taleghani’s update of Euripides’ tragedy at the National’s Olivier theatre is a crude and timid start for Indhu Rubasingham’s reign … This is the first time, in fact, that a debutant has taken over the Olivier stage. And after sitting through this travesty, I suspect it could well be the last. The actor Nima Taleghani’s update of The Bacchae, studded with ultra-crude, in-yer-face banter, is so leaden that it makes the average panto look like a treatise on existentialism. … Sad to say, Taleghani’s text has none of the wit and subtlety of those two productions.
